summary:
The "Sanctioning Tyrannical and Oppressive People within the Chinese Communist Party Act" or "STOP CCP Act" (H.R. 3334, 118th Congress) directs the President to impose blocking and visa-related sanctions on members of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and related persons determined to engage in specified conduct. The bill passed the House on September 25, 2024, and was referred to the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations.

Section 4(a) requires the President, not later than 30 days after enactment, to impose sanctions on: (1) members and alternate members of the CCP Central Committee determined to engage in sanctionable conduct; (2) members of any successor organization if the Central Committee is dissolved; (3) adult family members (including spouses and adult family members of spouses) of such persons; and (4) Chinese state-owned enterprises the President determines are illegally manufacturing or distributing fentanyl or knowingly manufacturing or distributing fentanyl precursor chemicals.

Section 4(b) defines sanctionable conduct as playing a significant role in developing or implementing government policies or laws the President determines appear designed to violate Hong Kong's autonomy; harass, intimidate, or increase aggression toward Taiwan; contribute to political oppression or human rights violations within the PRC (including of Uyghur Muslims); or willfully engage in malicious activities, including disinformation, to interfere with U.S. federal, state, or local elections.

Section 4(c) prescribes two sanction types: (A) blocking of property under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA, 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.); and (B) inadmissibility, visa ineligibility, and mandatory revocation of existing visas under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.; revocation per 8 U.S.C. 1201(i)). Exceptions apply to admissions required under the UN Headquarters Agreement and to authorized U.S. intelligence, law enforcement, and national security activities.

Section 4(d) applies IEEPA penalties (50 U.S.C. 1705(b)–(c)) to violations. Section 4(e) grants implementation authority under 50 U.S.C. 1702 and 1704; Section 4(f) requires implementing regulations within 30 days.

Section 4(g) permits renewable 60-day waivers upon certification, 15 days in advance, that the waiver is vital to national security. Section 4(h) authorizes termination 15 days after certification that either the PRC/CCP has ceased enumerated conduct (Uyghur genocide, Tibetan oppression, Taiwan aggression, Hong Kong interference, IP theft) or the sanctioned person has renounced CCP membership and remediated conduct (or ceased fentanyl activities). Section 4(i) sunsets the President's waiver and license authorities two years after enactment. Section 4(j) excludes authority to sanction the importation of goods. Section 4(k) defines "appropriate congressional committees." Sections 2 and 3 contain findings and a sense of Congress.
